title: Writing practice: Reports, discounts, friction, and trade
description: Eight writing tasks: continue a story, report survey results, explain a discount step by step, argue from experiment data, and write an announcement.

stimuli.title: Story starter
paragraphs: The bell above the door of the old repair shop rang, though nobody had come in. On the counter lay a small brown package with Dalia's name on it.
Your task is to write the next part of the story. Include a description of the setting, at least one line of dialogue, a problem, and an ending that shows how Dalia changed or what she learned.

stimuli.title: Home languages at Lakeview Middle School
stimuli.caption: A survey asked 150 students which language they speak most at home.

stimuli.title: A jacket on sale
paragraphs: A jacket has a regular price of $80. This week the store takes 25% off the regular price. After the discount, the store adds 6% sales tax to the sale price, not to the regular price.
A classmate asks, “How much will I pay at the register, and why do we take off the discount first?”

stimuli.title: How far a toy car rolled
stimuli.caption: A toy car rolled down the same ramp onto three surfaces. The table shows how far it rolled across each surface. Friction is a force that slows things down when two surfaces rub together. Rougher surfaces have more friction.

stimuli.title: Two villages
paragraphs: Hillside Village has many apple orchards. The villagers pick more apples than they can eat, but there is no clay near the village, so they have few pots and bowls.
Marsh Village has thick, good clay. The villagers make strong pots and bowls, but few fruit trees grow in the wet soil.
A trader walks between the two villages every month. To specialize means to focus on making or growing what you do best.

stimuli.title: Your notes from lunchtime
stimuli.caption: The school office asks a witness to write a short report when something happens in a hallway. These are your notes about what you saw today.
rows: Sam's water bottle fell near the stairs, and water spread across the floor.
Two students walked past the puddle.
Jin did not see the water and slipped, but he caught the railing and was not hurt.
You went to find Mr. Rivera, the hallway monitor.
Mr. Rivera put out a wet-floor sign, and a custodian mopped the floor.

stimuli.title: Science Fair Night: event details
stimuli.caption: Details for an event that the class website will announce to families.
rows: Students show their science projects to families and teachers
The school gym (enter by the east door)
Students, families, and neighbors; it is free
Project board, delivered by 3:30 p.m. that afternoon
The parent club will serve light snacks

stimuli.title: Kinds of triangles
stimuli.caption: Facts about three kinds of triangles. Every triangle has 3 sides and 3 angles.

items.stem: Continue the story in your own way. Put the events in an order that keeps the reader interested, and use details that show feelings instead of only naming them.

checklist: My story begins right after the starter.
I described the setting with specific details.
I included dialogue with quotation marks.
I showed a problem and how it was solved or how Dalia changed.
I used varied transitions and kept my verb tense consistent.
exemplar: Continues the starter coherently with a clear sequence of events
Develops the setting, Dalia's feelings, and a problem or turning point
Uses dialogue with quotation marks and speech verbs
Uses sensory and descriptive language, including figurative language where it fits
Ends by resolving the problem or showing what Dalia learned, with varied transitions and a consistent verb tense

support.clue: Ask yourself: What is in the package? Who sent it? What does Dalia want to do? Decide on one problem before you start writing.
support.frame: Dalia slowly ______ the package. Inside, she found ______. “______,” she said. At first, ______. Then ______. Suddenly, ______. In the end, ______, and Dalia realized ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different story. “Kai ran to the shore as the tide pulled back. “Is that a bottle?” he whispered. At first, he thought it was trash. Then he saw a rolled paper inside. Suddenly, a wave splashed his shoes, and he grabbed the bottle. In the end, the note led him to his grandfather's old boat, and Kai realized that stories can travel.” Notice the dialogue, the transitions, and an ending with a realization. Continue Dalia's story the same way.

items.stem: Write a report for the school newsletter about what the survey shows. Present the main results, compare at least three numbers, and explain what the data suggest about the school community.

checklist: I began with a topic sentence that tells what the survey studied.
I compared at least three numbers using words such as more than, fewer than, and twice as many.
I used accurate numbers.
I explained what the data suggest, using a careful word such as suggests or may.
I organized my ideas in a logical order.
exemplar: Introduces the survey and the group surveyed (150 students)
Reports that Spanish is the most common (62) and compares other numbers accurately (for example, 62 is more than twice 28, or French and Vietnamese are equal at 14)
Uses comparison and quantity language (more than, fewer than, the same as, a total of)
Draws a careful conclusion about the variety of languages in the school community
Organizes the report as introduction, findings, and conclusion in a formal newsletter register

support.clue: Find the largest and smallest numbers. Look for two languages with the same number. Then think about what the table says about the languages students bring to school.
support.frame: A survey of ______ students asked ______. The results show that ______ is the most common language, with ______ students. In contrast, ______. ______ and ______ each have ______ students. In total, ______. These results suggest that ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different survey. “A survey of 80 students asked which season they like best. The results show that summer is the most popular, with 35 students. In contrast, only 10 students chose winter. Spring has 17 students, and autumn has 18. These results suggest that most students prefer warm weather.” Notice the topic sentence, the comparisons, and the careful conclusion. Report on the language survey the same way.

facts: 62 + 28 + 14 + 14 + 8 + 24 = 150, which matches the number of students surveyed.
French and Vietnamese both have 14 students.

items.stem: Write a step-by-step explanation for your classmate. Show how to find the discount, the sale price, the tax, and the final total. Explain why the tax is calculated on the sale price.

checklist: I explained how to find 25% of $80.
I explained how to find the sale price.
I explained how to find 6% of the sale price and the final total.
I explained why the tax is calculated on the sale price.
I used order words such as first, next, then, and finally.
exemplar: Finds the discount: 25% of $80 is $20 (for example, 0.25 × 80)
Finds the sale price: $80 − $20 = $60
Finds the tax and the total: 6% of $60 is $3.60, so the total is $63.60
Explains that the tax applies to the amount the customer actually pays after the discount
Sequences the steps with transitions and says what each number represents, using accurate vocabulary (percent, discount, sale price, sales tax)

support.clue: Work in order: first the discount, then the new price, then the tax. At each step, say what the number means, such as the amount taken off or the price after the discount.
support.frame: First, I find the discount by ______. That is ______. Next, I ______ to find the sale price, which is ______. Then I find the tax by ______, so the tax is ______. Finally, I ______. The total is ______. The tax is calculated on ______ because ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different problem. “First, I find the tip by calculating 15% of $40, which is 0.15 × 40 = $6. Next, I add the tip to the bill to find the total: $40 + $6 = $46. I find the tip from the food price because the tip is a percent of the food price. The total is $46.” Notice that each step names what the number means. Explain the jacket the same way.

facts: 25% of 80 = 20, so the sale price is 80 − 20 = 60.
6% of 60 = 3.60, so the final total is 60 + 3.60 = 63.60.

items.stem: Write a claim about which surface has the least friction. Use the data in the table as evidence, and explain how the data support your claim.

checklist: I made a claim that names a surface.
I used numbers from the table.
I explained how the numbers show less friction.
I used the word friction and a connector such as because.
exemplar: Claim names the smooth floor as the surface with the least friction
Evidence: the car rolled 210 cm on the smooth floor compared with 85 cm on carpet and 40 cm on sandpaper
Reasoning: less friction slows the car less, so it rolls farther
Uses science vocabulary (friction, surface, force)
Links evidence to claim with a connector such as because or so

support.clue: Find the surface where the car rolled the farthest. Think: if friction slows the car, what does a long distance say about the friction?
support.frame: I claim that the ______ has the least friction. The evidence is that the car rolled ______ cm on the ______, but only ______ cm on the ______. This shows that ______ because ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different experiment. “I claim that the metal spoon carries heat best. The evidence is that the metal spoon felt hot after two minutes in warm water, but the wooden spoon felt only a little warm. This shows that metal carries heat faster because heat moves through it easily.” Notice the claim, the evidence, and the reason. Write about the toy car the same way.

facts: Friction is a force that opposes motion between surfaces that touch.
Rougher surfaces generally produce more friction.
Metals conduct heat faster than wood.

items.stem: Explain how trade could help both villages. Use the words specialize, trade, and benefit, and describe what each village gives and what each village gets.

checklist: I told what Hillside Village has and needs.
I told what Marsh Village has and needs.
I explained how both villages benefit from trade.
I used the words specialize, trade, and benefit.
I used cause-and-effect words.
exemplar: Identifies each village's extra goods and needs (apples and clay pots)
Explains the exchange: each village gives what it has plenty of and gets what it lacks
Uses economic vocabulary (specialize, trade, benefit) appropriately
Shows cause and effect: because each village focuses on what it does best, both have more goods
Writes a cohesive paragraph with connectors such as because, so, and as a result

support.clue: Make a chart in your mind: what does each village have too much of, and what does each village lack? Then think about what the trader carries in each direction.
support.frame: Hillside Village has ______, but it needs ______. Marsh Village has ______, but it needs ______. If they trade, Hillside Village can give ______ and get ______. Because each village can specialize in ______, both villages ______. As a result, ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different pair. “Lakeview School has a strong band but no art studio. Hilltop School has an art studio but no band. If they trade, Lakeview can give a concert and get art lessons. Because each school focuses on what it does best, both schools offer more to students. As a result, all the students benefit.” Notice what each side has, needs, and gets. Explain the two villages the same way.

facts: Specialization and trade can allow both sides to have more of the goods they need (basic economics, simplified).
The villages and their resources are fictional details supplied in the stimulus.

items.stem: Write a clear report for the school office that tells what happened in the order it happened. Use details from your notes, and write as a witness.

checklist: I wrote the events in the order they happened.
I answered who, what, where, and when.
I used past-tense verbs and time words.
I stayed factual and did not add information that was not in my notes.
I ended by telling how the problem was solved.
exemplar: Includes who, what, where, and when in an organized account
Puts the events in accurate chronological order with sequence words
Uses past-tense verbs, including passive forms where suitable (for example, the floor was mopped)
Keeps an objective, factual tone and invents no details
States the resolution (the sign was placed and the floor was mopped) in a formal register suited to the school office

support.clue: Read the notes in order. For each note, ask: who did something, what happened, and where? Then add time words to connect the notes.
support.frame: At lunchtime, ______ near ______. As a result, ______. After that, ______. Fortunately, ______. Next, I ______. Then ______. The problem was solved when ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different event. “During art class, a jar of paint tipped over near the sink. As a result, blue paint spread across the table. After that, a student noticed the mess and told the teacher. Then the teacher gave out paper towels. The problem was solved when the table was clean and dry.” Notice who, what, where, and the time words. Write your report the same way.

items.stem: Write an announcement for the class website that tells families about Science Fair Night. Include all the important information, and organize it so readers can find it easily.

checklist: I included what, when, where, and who can come.
I included what student presenters must bring and when.
I organized the information in a clear order.
I used a friendly, polite tone and ended with an invitation.
exemplar: Includes all key details accurately (the event, Thursday 6:00 to 7:30 p.m., the gym and east door, free, boards by 3:30 p.m.)
Organizes the information logically, with a topic sentence and grouped details
Uses a polite, welcoming register suited to families
Uses time and place expressions accurately (from, to, in, by)
Ends with a closing invitation or reminder

support.clue: Check the table for every detail a family needs: what the event is, when and where it happens, who can come, and what students must do. Decide in what order to tell them.
support.frame: Please join us for ______ on ______ from ______ to ______. The event will be held in ______. You can enter through ______. Everyone is welcome, including ______. Student presenters should ______ by ______. We hope to see you there!
support.model: Mentor example about a different event. “Please join us for the Spring Book Sale on Saturday from 9:00 to 12:00 in the library. You can enter through the front doors. Everyone is welcome, including families and neighbors. Volunteers should arrive by 8:30 to help set up tables. We hope to see you there!” Notice the event, the time, the place, who is invited, and a friendly ending. Write your announcement the same way.

facts: All event details are fictional details supplied in the table.

items.stem: Write a paragraph for a younger student that tells how the three kinds of triangles are alike and how they are different. Use the facts in the table.

checklist: I wrote a topic sentence about triangles.
I described the sides of each kind of triangle.
I told at least one way the triangles are alike and one way they are different.
I used math words such as equal, sides, and angles.
exemplar: Topic sentence introduces the three kinds of triangles
Accurate descriptions of the sides (all equal, at least two equal, none equal)
Includes angle information correctly (for example, the angles of an equilateral triangle are each 60°)
Names a similarity (3 sides and 3 angles) and differences, with contrast words such as while and but
Uses mathematical vocabulary (equilateral, isosceles, scalene, equal, angles)

support.clue: Read across each row of the table. Each kind of triangle has a name, a fact about sides, and a fact about angles. Think about what is the same for all three and what changes.
support.frame: All three kinds of triangles have ______. An equilateral triangle has ______, while an isosceles triangle has ______. A scalene triangle is different because ______. One way they are alike is ______.
support.model: Mentor example about different things. “All three vehicles have wheels. A bicycle has two wheels and no engine, while a motorcycle has two wheels and an engine. A car is different because it has four wheels and an engine. One way they are alike is that they carry people from place to place.” Notice the contrast words and the final similarity. Write about the triangles the same way.

facts: Every triangle has 3 sides and 3 angles.
An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides and 3 equal angles of 60° each.
An isosceles triangle has at least 2 equal sides and at least 2 equal angles.
A scalene triangle has no equal sides and no equal angles.
